claims.claimText: NUS policy states that verdicts from AI detection tools are not admissible as conclusive evidence in disciplinary processes to charge students with academic dishonesty or to penalize student work.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The verdicts of current AI tools purported to determine whether an analyzed input has been generated by AI are not admissible as conclusive evidence in a disciplinary process to charge a student with academic dishonesty or as justification to penalize student work.

claims.claimText: NUS policy states that representing AI output as one's own work without acknowledgement is plagiarism; students who submit AI-generated work without acknowledging its use can be sanctioned for academic dishonesty.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Representing an AI's output as your own work, without any acknowledgement that you have used such a tool, is plagiarism. A student found to have submitted work generated by AI but failed to acknowledge their use of AI can still be sanctioned for plagiarism, assuming the case can be made.
evidence.snippetLocation: 3. A General Message to Our Students; 2.6 Academic Dishonesty

claims.claimText: NUS states that instructors should be transparent about where and how they deploy AI in courses, including for generating content, virtual tutoring, and assessment feedback.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Instructors should be transparent about where and how they deploy AI in NUS courses. This is especially important where AI is deployed to generate course content (including assessment questions), to function as virtual tutors to answer student queries, or to help with assessment feedback and grading.
evidence.snippetLocation: 2.1 Be Transparent About the Use of AI

claims.claimText: NUS requires prior approval from Head of Department or relevant Deanery before using AI tools to provide instruction, feedback, or marks to students, submitted via an AI Risk Assessment.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: The use of AI tools to provide instruction to learners in the form of responses, feedback and/or marks, whether as virtual tutors or as markers, requires prior approval by Head of Department or relevant Deanery, under the oversight of Chair of the AI-COP. Approval must be sought through submission of an AI Risk Assessment.

claims.claimText: NUS policy sets the default assumption that AI tool use is permitted for unsupervised (take-home) assessments, provided use is duly acknowledged; assessments forbidding AI must be conducted in-person and instructor-supervised.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Conversely, the default assumption for any unsupervised (e.g., 'take home') assessment task is that the use of AI tools is permitted so long as the use is duly acknowledged. ... If the decision is that students should be forbidden from using AI tools for an assessment (for pedagogical reasons), then crucial aspects of that assessment should be conducted in-person and instructor-supervised.
evidence.snippetLocation: 2.5 Assessments Forbidding the Use of AI

snapshot.summary: At NUS, follow the specific assessment rule, acknowledge or cite AI use, use only NUS-approved tools when NUS data is involved, and do not treat an NUS service listing as blanket permission.

dimensions.summary: NUS treats unacknowledged AI output presented as a student’s own work as plagiarism and separately requires citation guidance to be followed. Scope: teaching-and-learning policy and student citation guidance.

do: Read the assignment instructions and acknowledge or cite AI use as required.
dont: Do not submit AI output as your own without acknowledgement.

dimensions.summary: NUS sets a default that AI use is permitted for unsupervised take-home assessments when acknowledged; assessments forbidding AI must be in-person and supervised. Scope: NUS policy, subject to the specific assessment.

do: Check whether the assessment is supervised and follow its stated AI rule.
dont: Do not assume the take-home default applies to an assessment with a contrary rule.

dimensions.summary: NUS requires citation of AI-generated content according to style conventions and treats unacknowledged AI output as plagiarism. Scope: student academic work.

do: Cite AI-generated content using the applicable style guidance.
dont: Do not omit acknowledgement when AI contributed to submitted work.

dimensions.summary: Where NUS data is involved, the NUS policy requires use of NUS-approved AI tools. Scope: NUS data, not every personal tool or every student task.

do: Use an NUS-approved tool when NUS data is involved.
dont: Do not upload NUS data to an unapproved AI service.

dimensions.summary: NUS records list institutional AI services and separately require NUS-approved tools when NUS data is involved. Provision or listing is not permission for a course or assessment.

do: Verify eligibility, data conditions, and the assessment rule before use.
dont: Do not infer student assessment permission from an NUS service listing.

heldClaims.claimText: Student disciplinary decisions under NUS Statute 6 feature two adjudication tiers with a general 14-day appeal clock under Regulation 10; detailed statutory exceptions, filing formalities, and start events remain UNVERIFIED pending full statute text.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
Students can choose to appeal within fourteen days after receiving notice of the decision made by the BOD (clause 25 of NUS Regulation 10 Discipline with Respect to Students).
Appeals are heard by the Disciplinary Appeals Board (DAB) chaired by a member from NUS Board of Trustees (BOT) and comprises two other members of the Senate.
